Senses.Explanation: The side position is the differentiated member of Caodong positional language: it is where forms, speech, and responsive activity are located in contrast with the straight position. Caoshan Benji identifies it with the realm in which myriad forms appear, then turns that classification into an interview test when an unnamed monastic interlocutor claims to come from the side position. Linquan Conglun preserves the refusal in his appraisal. Yongjue Yuanxian classifies merit and royal-son sequences as matters on this side while warning against mechanically mapping separate schemes together. Baiyu and Dahui Zonggao both expose a limit: diagrams and verbal explanations can themselves remain side-position talk. The term therefore names a relational position inside these attested schemes; it is not a general synonym for error, inferiority, or one physical side.

Senses.Explanation: A question-and-answer exchange is the public back-and-forth in which an asker puts something forward and a respondent must meet it. Zhaozhou's record makes the form perform itself: an unnamed monk asks how Zhaozhou answers when every question-and-answer falls within the thinking faculty, and Zhaozhou replies, “Ask.” Zhongfeng Mingben sharpens the reciprocity by saying that question lies in answer, answer lies in question, and question-and-answer race across one another. The records also use question-and-answer as a documentary and encounter label. Zhongfeng's compiler can write that the question-and-answer was not recorded, while the Record Continuing the Lamp narrates an exchange in which blows and shouts accompanied the participants and ordinary feelings fell away. Zen masters therefore keep the exchange public without equating its format with success. Juyun Chuiwan Guangzhen says a genuine question requires an apt answer and calls a mismatched pair deaf and blind to one another; Foyan Qingyuan rebukes people who simply take question-and-answer to be Zen. Yingshan Zhiyin likewise makes fluent question-and-answer conditional on being able to assess the exchanges already raised.

Senses.Explanation: To ask about the Way is to approach someone for instruction or put the matter into question. An emperor receives Huilin Zongben for such an audience, King Zhongyi invites Tiantai Deshao for it, and the Daoist Luo Zhaochang repeatedly comes to Yuwang Duanyu. Sikong Benjing refuses to let the purpose remain vague. He asks Yang Guangting whether he has come seeking Buddha or asking about the Way, and then answers the distinction the envoy cannot state.
